extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claims under 35 U.S.C. 101, implementing the Alice/Mayo two-part test and determining whether claims fall within the four statutory categories or are directed to judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) and, if so, whether they recite significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). Second, the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101. See MPEP § 2106.03 for the categories and MPEP § 2106.04–2106.05 for the Alice/Mayo analysis. Examiners are reminded that 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold inquiry and that 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, and 103 remain available tools for assessing patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories (Step 1): process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 defines four categories of invention: processes (actions or series of steps) and three categories of 'things'—machines, manufactures and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-process categories, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. A claim need only fall within at least one category. When in doubt, examine the entire disclosure and construe claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). See MPEP § 2106.03 for definitions and examples (e.g., microprocessor as manufacture; bicycle as both machine and manufacture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product must have physical/tangible form for machine/manufacture/composition
rubrics_metrics.description: For machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter, the claimed product must have a physical or tangible form to fall within a statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intangible collections of information or software expressed as code detached from any medium are not statutory products. If a product claim lacks physical structure or tangible form, it may fail Step 1 even if otherwise new and useful. See Digitech and Microsoft v. AT&T examples in MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claims that are not to any statutory category include products without physical form (data per se, computer program per se), transitory signals (propagating electrical/electromagnetic signals or carrier waves), and subject matter expressly prohibited by statute (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the BRI of a claim encompasses such non-statutory embodiments, the claim as a whole may be non-statutory and warrant rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility because BRI sets the boundaries of coverage and influences whether the claim seeks to cover subject matter outside the statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating eligibility based on the BRI also ensures eligibility does not depend on drafter's art. Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 and Step 2 (Alice/Mayo). Consult MPEP § 2111 for determining BRI. Examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, McRO, Amdocs) demonstrate how construing claim terms affects eligibility conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 evaluation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter (i.e., whether it falls within one or more statutory categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 as appropriate). If the BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim may fail Step 1 and examiner should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendment if possible. If claim falls within a statutory category (Step 1: YES), proceed to Step 2A (Alice/Mayo). See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2 overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2 is the Alice/Mayo test: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). If yes, Step 2B — determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the Alice/Mayo framework should be used for 35 U.S.C. 101 eligibility determinations. If Step 2A is NO, the claim is eligible without reaching Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.04 and § 2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions identification (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena; these concepts have also been described as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied concepts, mathematical algorithms, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no bright lines among the exceptions; it is sufficient that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. The examiner should identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception. The Supreme Court's preemption concern guides this inquiry. See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for natural products (2106.04(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing product claims that implicate nature-based subject matter, determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from any natural product (i.e., whether the claimed product exhibits characteristics that are markedly different in kind and not merely in degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product as a whole with the naturally occurring counterpart. The analysis looks to whether the claim recites features that give rise to new or enhanced properties or functionalities. See MPEP § 2106.04(c) and cases distinguishing products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'Significantly more' / inventive concept (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception under Step 2A, Step 2B asks whether the claim as a whole recites additional elements, individually or in combination, that amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an 'inventive concept' or practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether additional claim limitations integrate the exception into a practical application or provide an unconventional technical solution. The machine-or-transformation test is a useful clue to this inquiry but not a standalone test. See MPEP § 2106.05 for specific considerations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(a) — Improvements to computer functioning or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field can demonstrate 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim limitations provide an improvement in computer technology (e.g., improved data structure, enhanced processing) or solve a technological problem, this supports eligibility. Enfish and McRO are cited as examples where improvements supported eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(b) — Particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a particular machine (as opposed to a generic computer) can weigh in favor of eligibility if the machine limitation meaningfully limits the claim beyond merely linking the exception to a machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze whether the machine limitation is specific and integral (not a conventional or generic computer). The particular-machine consideration is one factor in the Step 2B analysis. See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(c) — Particular transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed transformation of an article to a different state or thing (a particular transformation) can support a 'significantly more' finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that meaningfully change the nature of an article (physical transformations) are relevant under Step 2B and are related to the machine-or-transformation analysis. See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(d) — Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the field do not, by themselves, supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting that a limitation is conventional, the examiner should support that assertion with evidence (references, common knowledge). Mere conclusory statements are insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for guidance on documentation and evaluation of conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(e) — Other meaningful limitations / unconventional ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Other limitations that meaningfully limit the judicial exception or that recite an unconventional ordered combination of elements may supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim recites limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application or produce an improvement. An unconventional combination that offers a technical solution supports eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) and cited Federal Circuit examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(f) — Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that only instruct practitioners to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (mere instructions to apply the exception) do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claim language is typically insufficient because it simply tells the user to implement the exception without adding meaningful limitations. See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(g) — Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant post-solution or extra-solution activity (trivial additional steps) does not render an otherwise ineligible claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify whether added activities are merely token extras that do not transform the exception into an inventive application. See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(h) — Field of use and technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting a claim to a particular field of use or technological environment, by itself, does not make a claim that is directed to an exception eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-of-use or environment limitations that are merely nominal may be disregarded for eligibility purposes. The limitation must meaningfully change the claim to provide significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(h) and the cited precedent that targeting the Internet or a particular field does not avoid abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as an indicator (not a separate test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue to eligibility but should not be used as a separate or sole test; it should be considered as part of the Step 2B 'significantly more' determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While M-O-T can be informative, do not treat it as conclusive. Use it alongside other Step 2B considerations. See MPEP § 2106 and Bilski and related case law discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern underlying the Alice/Mayo framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying concern driving the two-part framework is preemption — whether the claim effectively monopolizes a judicial exception and would prevent others from using basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although preemption is not a standalone statutory test, examiners should consider whether a claim's breadth would preempt use of the exception when analyzing Steps 2A and 2B. Cite relevant case law and factor preemption into eligibility rationale. See MPEP § 2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis and Pathways A/B/C (2106.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: The flowchart shows three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility; streamlined analysis), Pathway B (claim falls within a statutory category and is not directed to an exception — Step 2A: NO), and Pathway C (claim falls within a statutory category, is directed to an exception, but recites significantly more — Step 2A: YES; Step 2B: YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If eligibility is self-evident, use streamlined analysis (Pathway A). If uncertain whether a streamlined analysis applies, conduct a full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims found eligible at A but analyzed further will be found eligible at B or C. See MPEP § 2106.06 for examples of self-evident eligibility and clear improvements to technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility (2106.07(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the examiner must identify the judicial exception at issue, explain why the claim is directed to that exception (identify specific claim limitations), set forth the BRI, and explain why the additional limitations do not amount to significantly more — supporting factual findings with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs where applicable, cite the specification and prior art/evidence for conventionality, and explain the reasoning clearly to assist applicant's response. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for required content and examples of acceptable explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response to 101 rejection (2106.07(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: On receiving applicant's arguments or evidence in response to a 101 rejection, the examiner must evaluate whether the applicant has rebutted the factual bases of the rejection or shown error, and determine whether to maintain, withdraw, or reopen the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claim amendments, factual evidence submitted (e.g., declarations, references), and whether the examiner's characterization of the claim and the BRI were correct. Provide further explanation if maintaining the rejection. See MPEP § 2106.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are found eligible or in rejections (2106.07(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, examiners may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference portions of the specification that describe claimed improvements and note claim elements producing that improvement). Similarly, clarifying remarks may assist in explaining the rationale for a rejection (e.g., explaining the BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. They help applicants understand the examiner's rationale and suggested amendments. See MPEP § 2106.07(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 112/102/103) in conjunction with 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are reminded that 35 U.S.C. 101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, and 103 provide additional requirements and tools to ensure claims meet patentability conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim meets 101, it still must satisfy novelty, non-obviousness, enablement/written description, and other statutory requirements. Cite and apply these provisions as needed (see MPEP § 2103 and related sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation examples as guidance for eligibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent case law examples (e.g., Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, McRO, Amdocs) illustrate that claim interpretation — in light of the specification and BRI — can determine whether claims are mental processes/abstract ideas or improvements in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim terms in light of the specification and record; whether limitations require implementation (e.g., specific algorithms, specific machine limitations) can be determinative. Use these cases as analogies but analyze each claim on its facts. See MPEP § 2106 II and examples throughout § 2106.04–2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting conventionality and factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that claim elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional, examiners should support such findings with evidence from the specification, prior art, or other factual sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions that elements are conventional must be supported; unsupported conclusory statements are improper. When relying on common sense or routine-ness, document the rationale and any supporting citations. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) and 2106.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice to suggest amendments when BRI covers non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When the BRI of a claim covers non-statutory embodiments, the examiner should, as a best practice, point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice helps the applicant resolve eligibility issues and facilitates prosecution. Examples include narrowing machine-readable media claims to exclude carrier waves. See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.07(c).
